A fully connected layer connects every input to every neuron. For images, this is wasteful in two ways. It needs an enormous number of weights, and it ignores that pixels close to each other belong together and that a pattern means the same wherever it appears. Convolutional networks build these two assumptions into their layers. This section introduces the convolutional layer, the strides and padding that control its output size, pooling, the

Local Receptive Fields and Shared Weights

children.label: Local Receptive Fields and Shared Weights

children.value: Our eyes analyze a scene with receptive fields, small regions of the retina whose cells respond to local patterns, and the same kind of field works at every position of the visual field. A convolutional layer copies this design. Each neuron of the layer connects only to a small neighborhood of the input, for example

children.html: 5×55 \times 55×5

children.value: shows. The layer contains one such neuron for every position of the input, and all of them share the same weights and the same bias.

children.alt: A hidden neuron connected to a small patch of the input, its local receptive field.

children.value: A hidden neuron connected to a small patch of the input, its local receptive field.

Earlier systems prepared images for learning with hand-designed filters, such as Gaussian smoothing, Sobel gradients, or HOG descriptors, and fed the results into a network. This limited what the network could learn, and filters chosen for one task did not necessarily transfer to the next. A convolutional layer learns its filters from the data instead.

Sharing the weights has three consequences. The layer computes the same feature at every position, so a pattern is detected wherever it appears. The number of parameters is small and independent of the image size. And every weight receives an update from every position in each backward pass, since the shared weights collect the deltas of all positions like the shared bias in

Flattening ties the network to one input size, because the length of the vector depends on the size of the feature maps. Modern architectures replace it with global average pooling, which produces one value per feature map for any input size, followed by a single fully connected layer.
